title: Present Simple for Daily Habits
explanation: Use the present simple to talk about things you do regularly or routines. Add an 's' or 'es' at the end of the verb for he, she, or it.
example_correct: She walks to work every morning.
example_common_mistake: She walk to work every morning.

title: Articles: A, An, and The
explanation: Use 'a' before words starting with a consonant sound, and 'an' before vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u). Use 'the' when talking about a specific item.
example_correct: I ate an apple and a sandwich for lunch.
example_common_mistake: I ate a apple and an sandwich for lunch.

title: Simple Questions (What, Where, When)
explanation: Start your question with a question word like What, Where, or When, followed by do or does, and then the person.
example_correct: Where do you live?
example_common_mistake: Where you live?

title: Plural Nouns (Regular & Irregular)
explanation: Add 's' or 'es' to make most nouns plural. Some special words change completely, like child to children or person to people.
example_correct: Three children are playing in the park.
example_common_mistake: Three childs are playing in the park.

title: Possessive Adjectives (My, Your, His, Her)
explanation: Use my, your, his, her, our, and their to show who owns something. Place them right before the noun.
example_correct: This is her book on the table.
example_common_mistake: This is she book on the table.

title: Adjectives Before Nouns
explanation: In English, describe words (adjectives) always come before the thing they describe, not after.
example_correct: He drives a red car.
example_common_mistake: He drives a car red.

title: Prepositions of Place (In, On, At)
explanation: Use 'in' for enclosed spaces or cities, 'on' for surfaces, and 'at' for specific points or locations.
example_correct: She is sitting at her desk in the office.
example_common_mistake: She is sitting on her desk inside the office.

title: Can and Can't for Ability
explanation: Use 'can' to show you are able to do something, and 'can't' to show you cannot. Never add 'to' after can.
example_correct: I can speak English well.
example_common_mistake: I can to speak English well.

title: Imperatives for Simple Commands
explanation: Use the main action verb at the start of a sentence to give instructions or directions.
example_correct: Please open the window.
example_common_mistake: Please to open the window.

title: Past Simple for Finished Events
explanation: Use the past simple to talk about actions completed in the past. Regular verbs end with '-ed'.
example_correct: We visited London last summer.
example_common_mistake: We visit London last summer.

title: Present Continuous for Current Actions
explanation: Use am/is/are + verb ending in '-ing' for things happening right now or temporary situations.
example_correct: They are studying in the library right now.
example_common_mistake: They studying in the library right now.

title: Going To for Future Intentions
explanation: Use am/is/are + going to + verb when you have already planned to do something in the future.
example_correct: I am going to buy a new laptop tomorrow.
example_common_mistake: I going to buy a new laptop tomorrow.

title: Comparatives (-er / more)
explanation: Use '-er' for short words and 'more' for longer words when comparing two things, followed by 'than'.
example_correct: This phone is faster than my old one.
example_common_mistake: This phone is more fast than my old one.

title: Superlatives (-est / most)
explanation: Use 'the' plus '-est' or 'the most' to show something has the highest degree among three or more things.
example_correct: She is the smartest student in the class.
example_common_mistake: She is most smart student in the class.

title: Countable vs Uncountable Nouns
explanation: Use 'many' or 'few' for things you can count (apples). Use 'much' or 'little' for things you cannot count (water, money).
example_correct: I don't have much time today.
example_common_mistake: I don't have many time today.

title: Adverbs of Frequency (Always, Sometimes, Never)
explanation: Place frequency words before main verbs, but after the verb 'to be'.
example_correct: He is always punctual for meetings.
example_common_mistake: He always is punctual for meetings.

title: Modals of Obligation (Must, Should, Have to)
explanation: Use 'should' for advice, 'have to' for general rules, and 'must' for strong personal necessity.
example_correct: You should sleep early before your exam.
example_common_mistake: You should to sleep early before your exam.

title: First Conditional (Real Future Possibilities)
explanation: Use 'if' + present simple for the condition, and 'will' + verb for the future result.
example_correct: If it rains tomorrow, I will stay home.
example_common_mistake: If it will rain tomorrow, I stay home.

title: Present Perfect for Life Experience
explanation: Use have/has + past participle to talk about experiences without specifying the exact time in the past.
example_correct: I have visited Japan twice.
example_common_mistake: I have visit Japan twice in 2020.

title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
explanation: Use past simple for specific past times (yesterday). Use present perfect for general experience or unfinished time (this week).
example_correct: I saw him yesterday, but I haven't seen him today.
example_common_mistake: I have seen him yesterday.

title: Past Continuous vs Past Simple
explanation: Use past continuous (was/were -ing) for an ongoing background action interrupted by a shorter past simple action.
example_correct: I was cooking when the telephone rang.
example_common_mistake: I cooked when the telephone was ringing.

title: Second Conditional (Hypothetical Situations)
explanation: Use 'if' + past simple, followed by 'would' + base verb to talk about imaginary present or future situations.
example_correct: If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.
example_common_mistake: If I will have more time, I will learn Spanish.

title: Reported Speech Basics
explanation: When telling someone what another person said, shift present tense verbs into past tense.
example_correct: He said that he was busy.
example_common_mistake: He said that I am busy.

title: Passive Voice in Simple Tenses
explanation: Focus on the action or object rather than who performed it by using form of 'be' + past participle.
example_correct: The report was submitted by the team.
example_common_mistake: The report submitted by the team.

title: Relative Clauses (Who, Which, That)
explanation: Use 'who' for people and 'which' or 'that' for things to connect two sentences smoothly.
example_correct: The manager who hired me is very supportive.
example_common_mistake: The manager which hired me is very supportive.

title: Gerunds vs Infinitives (Enjoy doing vs Decide to do)
explanation: Some verbs are followed by '-ing' (enjoy, avoid), while others take 'to' + base verb (decide, plan).
example_correct: I enjoy working on creative projects.
example_common_mistake: I enjoy to work on creative projects.

title: Used To for Past Habits
explanation: Use 'used to' + base verb for states or routines that were true in the past but are no longer true now.
example_correct: I used to live in Chicago.
example_common_mistake: I was used to live in Chicago.

title: Present Perfect Continuous (Duration of Action)
explanation: Use have/has been + verb-ing to highlight how long an action has been happening up to the present moment.
example_correct: She has been working here for three years.
example_common_mistake: She is working here since three years.

title: Third Conditional (Past Regrets)
explanation: Use 'if' + past perfect, followed by 'would have' + past participle to talk about imaginary past events.
example_correct: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
example_common_mistake: If I studied harder, I would pass the exam.

title: Modals of Deduction (Must have, Might have, Could have)
explanation: Use modal + have + past participle to guess or express certainty about something in the past.
example_correct: He must have forgotten about the meeting.
example_common_mistake: He must forgot about the meeting.

title: Advanced Connectors (However, Nevertheless, Whereas)
explanation: Use formal transition words to contrast ideas across professional sentences.
example_correct: Sales were low; nevertheless, profits remained high.
example_common_mistake: Sales were low whereas profits remained high.

title: Passive Voice in Formal & Professional Contexts
explanation: Use passive forms with modals or continuous tenses to sound objective in business reports.
example_correct: The strategic proposal is being reviewed by the board.
example_common_mistake: The strategic proposal is reviewing by the board.

title: Phrasal Verbs in Business English
explanation: Master common multi-word verbs like 'carry out', 'bring up', or 'look into' in professional speech.
example_correct: We will look into the customer issue immediately.
example_common_mistake: We will look the customer issue immediately.

title: Wish & If Only for Unreal Desires
explanation: Use 'wish' + past simple for present desires, or 'wish' + past perfect for past regrets.
example_correct: I wish I had double-checked the numbers.
example_common_mistake: I wish I check the numbers.

title: Participle Clauses for Concise Writing
explanation: Combine two clauses into one using '-ing' or '-ed' forms to make your sentences flow smoothly.
example_correct: Having finished the report, she sent the email.
example_common_mistake: Finished the report, she sent the email.

title: Causative Verbs (Have / Get something done)
explanation: Use have or get + object + past participle when someone else performs a service for you.
example_correct: I had my presentation slides reviewed yesterday.
example_common_mistake: I reviewed my presentation slides yesterday by someone.

title: Inversion for Emphasis
explanation: Place negative words like 'rarely', 'seldom', or 'not only' at the start of a sentence and swap verb and subject for dramatic emphasis.
example_correct: Rarely have I seen such dedication.
example_common_mistake: Rarely I have seen such dedication.

title: Mixed Conditionals
explanation: Combine past condition with present result (or vice versa) to express complex hypothetical realities.
example_correct: If I had accepted that offer, I would be living in Tokyo today.
example_common_mistake: If I accepted that offer, I will live in Tokyo today.

title: Subjunctive Mood in Formal Requests
explanation: Use the base form of the verb after verbs like demand, insist, or recommend in formal statements.
example_correct: The director recommended that he attend the summit.
example_common_mistake: The director recommended that he attends the summit.

title: Advanced Cleft Sentences (What / It is... that)
explanation: Use 'What...' or 'It is...' structure to highlight the exact key point you want your audience to remember.
example_correct: What surprised us most was his thorough analysis.
example_common_mistake: Which surprised us most was his thorough analysis.

title: Complex Nominal Phrases
explanation: Pack detailed ideas efficiently into noun phrases for academic or executive communication.
example_correct: The unexpected decline in quarterly revenue triggered a audit.
example_common_mistake: The revenue declined unexpectedly in quarterly triggered a audit.

title: Ellipsis & Substitution
explanation: Omit repeated words smoothly to create concise, sophisticated conversational flow.
example_correct: She promised to complete the project, and did so by Friday.
example_common_mistake: She promised to complete the project, and completed the project by Friday.

title: Advanced Hedging & Diplomatic Tone
explanation: Use cautious language like 'it would appear that' or 'tend to' to discuss sensitive topics professionally.
example_correct: It would seem that the initial estimates were slightly optimistic.
example_common_mistake: The initial estimates were completely wrong.

title: Discourse Markers for Professional Debates
explanation: Use advanced transition phrases like 'be that as it may' or 'to put it another way' in meetings.
example_correct: Be that as it may, we must remain focused on quality.
example_common_mistake: Be that like it is, we must remain focused on quality.

title: Mastery of Complex Phrasal Prepositional Verbs
explanation: Use three-word phrasal verbs smoothly (e.g., 'come up against', 'cut back on', 'look forward to').
example_correct: We must cut back on unnecessary operational expenses.
example_common_mistake: We must cut back of unnecessary operational expenses.
